title: Harbour basics
blurb: Six everyday pictures: three camera-made, three AI-generated. Learn the four steps.

pictures.title: Earth from space
pictures.arrival: A gull drops a crumpled postcard on the noticeboard.
pictures.claim: NASA's famous "photo" of Earth is CGI. Wake up!
pictures.madeWith: Hasselblad film camera, by the Apollo 17 crew (NASA), 1972

wren.text: See how the clouds go soft and grainy in the dark ocean? Old film does that. My hunch is camera, but space pictures have fooled me before.

pip.text: It's TOO perfect. It looks like a computer wallpaper. I think a computer made it!

moss.text: That's the famous one, isn't it? People have argued over it for years. Don't take my word or theirs. Find out where it first came from.

jim.text: AI. Obviously. They've been faking space pictures since before computers existed. Don't ask me how. That's exactly what they want you to ask.

tide.headline: A long trail back to 1972
tide.body: Thousands of older copies wash up. The oldest leads to NASA's archive: frame AS17-148-22727, taken by the Apollo 17 crew on 7 December 1972, on film.

seal.headline: No seal
seal.body: It was shot on film in 1972, decades before content credentials existed. A missing seal tells you nothing here.

crate.headline: Labels stripped
crate.body: 1599 × 1600 pixels. Camera: not recorded. Date: not recorded. Somewhere along the way this copy lost its labels.

cues.note: Africa, Arabia and Madagascar, with fine, irregular coastlines
Cloud swirls with messy detail all the way down
Almost fully lit: the Sun was behind the crew

pictures.verdict: Camera-made. This is a film photograph taken by the Apollo 17 crew. Looks alone couldn't settle it. It really does look "too perfect".
pictures.lesson: The trail back to the original archive settled it, not the pixels.
pictures.source: NASA / Apollo 17 crew, 7 December 1972, frame AS17-148-22727. Public domain.

pictures.title: Cat in a hat
pictures.arrival: A message in a bottle bobs up against the harbour wall.
pictures.claim: My cat Biscuit at his first photoshoot!! 😻

wren.text: Golden glow, every whisker sharp, background melted to honey. That's a lot of perfect in one frame. It leans AI to me, but good photographers do exist!

pip.text: Look at the hat! It has two bumps on top like the ears are inside it. But the ears are ALSO folded down by the face. Where do the ears go?

moss.text: Says it's someone's cat, Biscuit. Fine. Then where are the other photos of Biscuit? Real pets have a hundred blurry ones.

jim.text: AI, like everything else. See? Right again. I'm always right. Well, I'm always saying the same thing, which is nearly the same.

tide.headline: Traced to a content credentials example
tide.body: The oldest copy washes up in the Content Authenticity Initiative's public set of example pictures, labelled "Generated by Adobe Firefly". It was never anybody's pet.

seal.headline: This copy lost its seal
seal.body: The original file carries a content credentials seal saying an AI tool made it. This copy was re-saved along the way, and the seal fell off. A missing seal doesn't mean a picture is real.

crate.headline: Labels stripped
crate.body: 2000 × 1556 pixels. Camera: not recorded. Date: not recorded. No labels either way.

cues.note: Dents in the hat's crown, as if ears were under it
But the ears are also folded down, merging into the brim's shadow
A flawless golden glow, like a studio dream
Whiskers that fade out in mid-air

pictures.verdict: AI-generated, by Adobe Firefly. The hat that seems to hold the ears twice and the too-perfect glow were clues, but the trail to the original, sealed file settled it.
pictures.lesson: Seals help when they survive. When they don't, following the trail back to the original can find one.
pictures.source: Adobe Firefly example image (Firefly_tabby_cat.jpg) from the C2PA / Content Authenticity Initiative example assets, https://contentauth.github.io/example-assets/ (MIT licence). The original file carries content credentials.

pictures.title: Cat at the window
pictures.arrival: Pip runs up waving a phone. "Someone posted this in the village chat!"
pictures.claim: Neighbour's cat caught peeking in at dusk 👀
pictures.madeWith: Phone camera, by Dr Sam Martin

wren.text: Motion blur on the cat, warm lamp light inside, dusk blue outside. It's messy, but the light behaves the way light does. Leans camera.

pip.text: There's a sticker on the glass, a little apple! Is it on the window or on the cat?? And there's a laptop at the bottom. So weird.

moss.text: Who'd bother faking a blurry cat? Nobody's selling anything or stirring anyone up. Doesn't prove it's real, mind.

jim.text: That blur? That's what AI does to hide its mistakes. Fake. Everything's fake these days, mark my words.

tide.headline: Nothing comes back
tide.body: No older copies at all. That's normal for a personal phone snap. Most real photos have no trail.

seal.headline: No seal
seal.body: Most phones weren't adding content credentials when this was taken.

crate.headline: Labels stripped
crate.body: 1500 × 2000 pixels, phone-shaped. Camera: not recorded. Date: not recorded. Chat apps usually strip these when you share.

cues.note: A sticker on the glass, sharp in front of the blurred cat. The layers line up.
Motion blur in the direction the cat moved
Room reflections overlapping the brick outside
A laptop edge: an ordinary, unposed moment

pictures.verdict: Camera-made: a real phone photo. Every check came back empty, with no copies, no seal and no labels.
pictures.lesson: For everyday photos, no trail is normal. Look at whether the scene hangs together and who shared it.
pictures.source: Personal photo by Dr Sam Martin, taken on a phone camera. A real, unedited photo.

pictures.title: Washing machine for sale
pictures.arrival: Moss pins a page from the island classifieds to the board.
pictures.claim: FOR SALE: washing machine, works fine, collection only. £40.
pictures.madeWith: Phone camera, by Dr Sam Martin

wren.text: Flat, harsh light, a slightly tilted phone angle, a mop in the corner. That's exactly how real listings look. Camera.

pip.text: I can read everything! The programme list, the "1000", the number on the sticker. All the little icons line up.

moss.text: Selling a used washer? Who'd invent that. But check the seller as well as the picture. Scams use real photos too.

jim.text: A washing machine? That's exactly what an AI would make to seem ordinary. Too ordinary. Suspicious.

tide.headline: No copies elsewhere
tide.body: No older copies. If this exact photo were on ten other listings, that would be a warning sign. It isn't.

seal.headline: No seal
seal.body: Most phones weren't adding content credentials when this was taken.

crate.headline: Labels stripped
crate.body: 1500 × 2000 pixels, phone-shaped. Camera: not recorded. Date: not recorded.

cues.note: Small printed text that reads properly
A sticker with a real-looking phone number
A mop in the corner: ordinary household mess
Floor tiles with straight, consistent lines

pictures.verdict: Camera-made. Everyone agreed, and they were right. Readable text and ordinary mess support a camera, but they don't prove it. Newer AI tools can write clean text too.
pictures.lesson: Real photos can still be used in scams. Check the claim and the seller as well as the picture.
pictures.source: Personal photo by Dr Sam Martin, taken on a phone camera. A real, unedited photo.

pictures.title: Rowan refuses the vaccine
pictures.arrival: A soggy flyer washes up on the beach.
pictures.claim: Look what they're putting in kids' books now!! What are they hiding??

wren.text: The sun is setting behind the fox, yet its face is lit brightly from the front. Light can't come from two places like that. It's a painting, and a very smooth one.

pip.text: All the words are spelled right, so maybe it's a real book? But the little bottle has no label at all. Real medicine always has a label!

moss.text: "What are they hiding?" That isn't a story, it's a question built to make you worried. When a picture is trying hard to scare me, I want to know who made it.

jim.text: AI, of course. Everything is. Don't trust any of it. Don't trust me either. Actually, do trust me.

tide.headline: There is no such book
tide.body: No book with this title turns up from any publisher or bookshop. The trail leads back to the SDA Vision workshops, where it was made with AI as an example of fake children's book covers that spread false health claims.

seal.headline: No seal
seal.body: This copy has no content credentials. It has been re-saved as a small web picture, and seals rarely survive that.

crate.headline: Labels stripped
crate.body: 1075 × 1154 pixels. Camera: not recorded. Date: not recorded. No labels either way.

cues.note: A vial with no label or maker: nothing you could check
The raised paw is lit from the front, though the sun sets behind
"What are they hiding?": a question designed to worry you
Crisp, correct title text. Modern AI writes clean text, so this proves nothing.

pictures.verdict: AI-generated. It was made for the SDA Vision workshops to copy a real trend: fake children's book covers that spread false health messages. No such book exists.
pictures.lesson: Ask what a picture wants you to feel, then check whether the thing it shows (here, a book) exists at all.
pictures.source: Image generated using OpenAI’s image-generation tool in ChatGPT, 8 October 2026. Prompt developed collaboratively by Dr Sam Martin and ChatGPT, for the SDA Vision workshops.

pictures.title: Hospital protest comic
pictures.arrival: The ferry brings a stack of newspapers. This picture is on the front page.
pictures.claim: Huge protest outside the hospital yesterday!
pictures.madeWith: Google Gemini and ChatGPT (OpenAI image generation)

wren.text: Everyone is lit the same, from nowhere in particular. Every face is equally sharp, front row and back. That's an illustration, and maybe an AI one.

pip.text: Most of the words are fine, but the little protest sign says "Chloe Dubois Buy Chloe"? That's nonsense! There's a logo in the corner too.

moss.text: The paper says this happened yesterday, but it's a drawing! Who's Chloe Dubois? And a logo tells you who posted it, not how it was made.

jim.text: A drawing pretending to be the news? AI. And the news is AI. And the newspaper. And probably the ferry.

tide.headline: Traced to workshop materials
tide.body: It traces back to the SDA Vision research workshops. The researcher who made it used AI image tools to create an example for teaching. It was never a news photo.

seal.headline: No seal
seal.body: No credentials on this copy. A logo in the corner is not a seal: anyone can paste a logo.

crate.headline: Labels stripped
crate.body: 1087 × 607 pixels. No camera, no date, no labels.

cues.note: A sign that reads "Chloe Dubois Buy Chloe": garbled text
Fluent speech bubbles. AI text is often good now.
Every face evenly lit and equally sharp
A logo shows who shared it, not how it was made

pictures.verdict: AI-generated. It's an illustration made for SDA Vision workshops, not a record of a real protest.
pictures.lesson: The biggest problem here wasn't the AI. It was the caption claiming the picture showed a real event.
pictures.source: Created by Dr Sam Martin for the SDA Vision workshops, using a mix of OpenAI’s image-generation tool in ChatGPT and Google Gemini.
